reckoner.distinguishingFeature: Creates and uses cognitive conflict within a single lesson.
reckoner.bestScienceFit: Discrepant events with a clear, visible outcome: dissolving and mass, falling objects, living and non-living, hygiene and microbes.
reckoner.commonPitfall: Running the demonstration before predictions are committed in writing, or skipping the explain step.
reckoner.evidenceSummary: Widely used as a diagnostic and conceptual-change strategy; evidence is mainly classroom-based. Anomalous data does not change ideas on its own, so the explain step carries the learning.

introduction.lead: A Predict–Observe–Explain puts students' own ideas on the line in a single lesson, then uses what they see to make those ideas open to change.
introduction.purposeStatement:
This guide helps undergraduate and early career teachers choose, run and follow up a POE in
NSW Science 7–10. A POE is a strategy, not a unit: it usually sits inside a larger model such as
5E, most often in Engage. The guide covers what makes an event genuinely discrepant, how to protect
the prediction from cueing, and how to turn surprise into revised explanations.
introduction.audience: Pre-service teachers in secondary science method units, and teachers in their first years.

theory.summary:
Students hold intuitive explanations that feel right because they usually work. A POE asks students to
use those explanations to predict, then confronts the prediction with an observation it cannot
explain. The surprise creates a reason to change, and the explain step gives students the chance to
build something better.

foundations.idea: A mismatch between expectation and experience creates the pressure for mental models to change.
foundations.designImplication: The event must reliably contradict the most common prediction, or there is no mismatch to work with.

foundations.idea: Dissatisfaction with a current idea is a precondition for adopting a new one.
foundations.designImplication: The predict step makes students commit to the current idea, so the observation can produce dissatisfaction with it.

foundations.idea: Learners improve when they notice and monitor their own thinking.
foundations.designImplication: Written predictions with reasons give students a record of their earlier thinking to compare against.

critiques.claim: Students often ignore, reject or reinterpret anomalous data rather than change their ideas.
critiques.response:
Choose events with unambiguous outcomes, let students check the observation themselves, and
treat the explain step, not the surprise, as where learning happens. Plan a follow-up, because one
POE rarely produces lasting change.

roles.teacher: Chooses a genuinely discrepant event, protects the prediction from cueing, makes the observation clear and checkable, and orchestrates reconciliation before consolidating the science.
roles.learner: Commits to a prediction with reasons, observes carefully, compares prediction with observation, and revises their explanation.

sequence.summary:
Three phases in one episode of about 20–50 minutes. A common variant, Predict–Explain–Observe–Explain,
asks students to explain their prediction before observing.
sequence.diagramMermaid:
flowchart LR A[Predict
with reasons] --> B[Observe
and record] --> C[Explain
and reconcile]
sequence.scaleNote: A POE is a single episode that sits inside a unit model, most often the Engage phase of a 5E sequence. It is not a unit architecture.

phases.name: Predict
phases.job: Get every student to commit, in writing, to a prediction and the reason for it.
essentialFeatures: An event chosen because it contradicts a common alternative conception
Individual written predictions before any discussion
No cueing of the expected answer through wording, tone or set-up
teacherMoves: Asks for a prediction and a reason

lookFors.question: Is the event likely to contradict the most common prediction?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Chosen from a documented alternative conception; many students will predict wrongly.
lookFors.weakEvidence: Most students will predict correctly, so there is no conflict.

lookFors.question: Does every student commit individually, in writing, before observing?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Written predictions are collected or displayed before the event runs.
lookFors.weakEvidence: A few students call out predictions orally.

lookFors.question: Are students asked why, not just what?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Prediction sheets require a reason for each prediction.

lookFors.question: Is the set-up free of cues to the expected answer?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Neutral wording and presentation; no hint of the surprise.
lookFors.weakEvidence: The teacher's framing signals the "right" answer.

examples.title: Which lands first?
examples.body:
The teacher holds a basketball and a tennis ball at the same height and asks each student to write
which will land first and why. The same is then asked of a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled one.
Predictions are tallied on the board without comment.
examples.diagnosis: A reliable discrepant event, individual written commitment with reasons, and a neutral set-up.

examples.title: "Let's see if the heavy one really is faster"
examples.body:
The teacher says "Most people think heavier things fall faster; let's see if that's true", then asks
for a show of hands.
examples.diagnosis: The framing cues that the common idea is wrong, and hands-up commits nobody to a reason.

examples.title: Will burning make it lighter?
examples.body:
A loose ball of steel wool sits on a digital balance under the visualiser. The teacher records
the mass, says the wool will be heated and then weighed again, and asks every student to write
down what the balance will read afterwards and why. No hint is given that anything unusual is
coming. The slips are collected before anything is lit. Most of the class predicts the mass
will drop, because burning uses the material up. The teacher tallies the predictions on the
board without comment on any of them. Safety: teacher demonstration only, with eye protection,
tongs and a heatproof mat, and the ignition source kept away from the balance until the first
mass has been recorded.
examples.diagnosis:
Burning steel wool gains mass, which contradicts what most of a Year 7 class will predict, so
poe-discrepant holds. Collecting written slips before the demonstration runs is
poe-commit-written, and requiring a reason is what makes the underlying idea available to work
on later (poe-reasons). The flat set-up, with no signal that the obvious answer is wrong,
keeps poe-no-cueing intact.

examples.title: Telling them the answer is surprising
examples.body:
The teacher sets up the same demonstration and opens with, "Most people think burning always
makes something lighter, so let's find out whether that is true." Hands go up for lighter,
then a scattering for heavier once the framing lands. The teacher counts the hands, heats the
wool and weighs it again, and the result gets the reaction it deserves. Nobody has written
anything down, and nobody has been asked why they chose what they chose.
examples.diagnosis:
The opening signals that the obvious answer is wrong, so what follows is a guess at what the
teacher wants rather than the student's own thinking, and poe-no-cueing fails. A show of hands
commits nobody in writing (poe-commit-written) and collects no reasons (poe-reasons), leaving
no record of the idea for the explain phase to work against.

phases.name: Observe
phases.job: Let every student see, record and check what actually happens.
essentialFeatures: Every student can see the event clearly, or runs it themselves
Observations are kept separate from interpretations
The event can be repeated if students doubt the result

lookFors.question: Can every student see and check the outcome?
lookFors.strongEvidence: A visualiser, small-group sets or repeat runs make the result unambiguous.
lookFors.weakEvidence: A front-bench demonstration half the class cannot see.

lookFors.question: Do students record observations before discussing them?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Observation boxes are completed before any talk about why.

lookFors.question: Are observations kept separate from inferences?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Students distinguish what they saw from what they think it means.
lookFors.weakEvidence: Explanations are written as if they were observations.

examples.title: The balance reading everyone can see
examples.body:
Salt is dissolved in water on a balance shown through a visualiser. Students record the reading before
and after, then write one observation and, separately, one inference. The teacher repeats the
weighing when a student suggests the balance is faulty.
examples.diagnosis: A visible, checkable result with observation and inference kept apart, and doubt answered with a repeat.

examples.title: The teacher tells them what they saw
examples.body: The demonstration runs on the front bench, and the teacher says "So you can see the mass didn't change."
examples.diagnosis: Students cannot check the result, and narration replaces their own observation, so doubt goes unaddressed.

examples.title: Why does the Moon change shape?
examples.body:
Each student holds a polystyrene ball at arm's length, with one lamp at the front of a
darkened room. Turning slowly on the spot, they stop at each quarter turn and sketch the lit
part of the ball as they see it from where they stand. Observations go in one column of the
sheet and what they think it means in another. Several students say the classroom lights are
spoiling the effect, so the teacher closes the blinds and the class runs it again. One student
notices that her own head never casts a shadow on the ball at first quarter, and says so. The
teacher tells the class that next lesson they will look at how Moon and sky knowledge sits in a
local seasonal calendar, a session being planned with the school's Aboriginal Education staff
and local Aboriginal community.
examples.diagnosis:
Every student sees the terminator from their own position instead of watching one
demonstration, and re-running it with the blinds down answers the doubt rather than
overriding it: both are poe-observe-visible. Sketching at each quarter turn before any
discussion meets poe-observe-record, and the two-column sheet holds poe-observe-inference.
The student noticing no shadow has produced exactly the observation the explain phase needs.

examples.title: One ball at the front bench
examples.body:
The teacher holds the only ball beside a lamp at the front bench and turns it slowly,
describing what happens as she goes. "You can see the shape changing, and notice there is no
shadow from the Earth falling across it, so phases are not an eclipse." Students copy a
labelled diagram from the board into their books. Two students at the back cannot see the lit
side of the ball from where they are sitting, and do not say so. Nobody records what they saw,
because the teacher has already said what it means.
examples.diagnosis:
Only the front of the room can check the result, so poe-observe-visible fails for the students
who most need it. The narration supplies the observation and its meaning together, before
anyone writes anything down, which breaks poe-observe-record and removes the mismatch the
explain phase runs on.

phases.name: Explain
phases.job: Help students reconcile prediction with observation and build a better explanation.
essentialFeatures: Students compare their prediction with the observation explicitly
Students revise their explanation before the teacher gives the science
The teacher consolidates the scientific explanation and names the alternative conception
A follow-up is planned, because one POE rarely produces lasting change
teacherMoves: Asks students to compare prediction and observation
formativeChecks: Exit ticket: I predicted… I observed… Now I think…

lookFors.question: Do students explicitly compare their prediction with the observation?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Students write or say what matched, what did not, and why.
lookFors.weakEvidence: The class moves straight to the answer.

lookFors.question: Do students revise their own explanations before the teacher explains?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Revised explanations are drafted in pairs, then shared.

lookFors.question: Does the teacher consolidate the science and name the alternative conception?
lookFors.strongEvidence: The scientific explanation is made explicit and contrasted with the common idea.
lookFors.weakEvidence: The episode ends with surprise but no resolution.

lookFors.question: Is the POE connected to later learning?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Predictions are kept and revisited, and the next lessons build on the conflict.
lookFors.weakEvidence: A one-off demonstration with nothing after it.

examples.title: Yeast: powder or organism?
examples.body:
Many students predicted that yeast would not inflate a balloon because "it's just a powder". In pairs
they compare their prediction with the inflated balloon and draft a new explanation. The teacher then
consolidates: yeast is a living, single-celled fungus that uses sugar and releases carbon dioxide.
Predictions are kept for the next lesson on cells.
examples.diagnosis: Explicit reconciliation, student revision before consolidation, and a planned follow-up.

examples.title: "Who got it right?"
examples.body: The teacher asks who predicted correctly, praises them, gives the explanation, and moves to the next topic.
examples.diagnosis: The POE becomes a quiz. Students who predicted wrongly feel judged, and nobody revises their thinking.

examples.title: A dome of ice above the lid
examples.body:
A sealed container filled to the brim with water came out of the freezer this morning with its
lid pushed off and a dome of ice standing proud of the rim. Most of the class had predicted the
water would shrink, because cooling makes things contract. In pairs, students write what they
predicted, what they can see, and what would have to be true for both. Several arrive at water
taking up more room as ice. The teacher then consolidates: water is unusual, expanding by about
a tenth as it freezes because of the open structure ice forms, and she names the idea that
everything shrinks when it cools rather than leaving it unspoken. She finishes by asking what
that would do to water sitting in a crack in a rock through a frosty night, and keeps the
prediction slips for next lesson.
examples.diagnosis:
Pairs compare prediction with observation and say what would have to be true for both, so
poe-reconcile and poe-revise happen before any teaching. The teacher then consolidates and
names the alternative conception directly, which is poe-consolidate. Asking about water in a
rock crack, and keeping the slips, turns a one-off demonstration into the opening of the
weathering sequence (poe-followup).

examples.title: Explained before anyone revises
examples.body:
The same container comes out of the freezer with its lid pushed off, and there is a good
reaction from the class. The teacher explains straight away that water is unusual because ice
forms an open structure held by hydrogen bonds, and that it expands by about nine per cent as
it freezes. It is a clear and correct explanation, and students copy it into their books.
Nobody is asked to compare it with what they predicted. The lesson ends with the container back
on the bench, and rock, frost and weathering are not mentioned.
examples.diagnosis:
The science is right but it arrives before students have done anything with their own
prediction, so poe-revise never happens and the idea the demonstration was chosen to unsettle
is left standing. With no link made to frost in a rock crack, poe-followup fails too, and a
strong discrepant event stays a curiosity about ice instead of becoming geological change.

workedSequences.title: Is yeast alive?
workedSequences.bigQuestion: How can we tell whether something is alive?
learningIntentions: Living things carry out life processes, such as using food and releasing gases
Yeast is a living, single-celled organism
targetConceptions: Living things must be visible and move

steps.activity:
Show three flasks of warm water with balloons on top: yeast and sugar; yeast only; sugar only.
Students write, individually, which balloons will inflate and why.
steps.formativeCheck: Written predictions with reasons

scaffoldSlots.prompt: Which alternative conception would a student reveal by predicting that only the sugar flask changes?

steps.activity: Pairs share predictions; the class tallies predictions for each flask without discussing the answer.
steps.formativeCheck: Class tally displayed

steps.activity:
Flasks stand in a warm water bath. Students record balloon size every five minutes and note any foam,
keeping observations separate from explanations.
steps.formativeCheck: Observation tables checked for separation of observation and inference

steps.activity:
Pairs compare predictions with observations and draft revised explanations. The teacher consolidates:
yeast is a living, single-celled fungus that uses sugar and releases carbon dioxide, which is why only
one balloon inflated.
steps.formativeCheck: Revised explanations shared

steps.activity: Exit ticket: "I predicted… I observed… Now I think…"
steps.formativeCheck: Exit tickets sorted to plan the next lesson

whyItWorks: The yeast-only and sugar-only flasks act as controls, so students can pin the change on yeast using sugar
The idea of yeast as powder is common and reliably contradicted
Observations are recorded over time, so the result builds and cannot be missed
The exit ticket gives the teacher evidence to plan the follow-up
workedSequences.watchFor: Warm water that is too hot will kill the yeast and remove the effect. Test the set-up beforehand.
workedSequences.predictPrompt: Before reading on, why are there three flasks rather than one? What would students be unable to conclude with only the yeast-and-sugar flask?

workedSequences.title: Which handwashing method removes the most "germs"?
workedSequences.bigQuestion: How well do everyday hygiene methods reduce the spread of disease?
learningIntentions: Hygiene practices reduce transmission of pathogens in different ways
Scientific models have strengths and limitations
targetConceptions: A quick rinse with water is enough
All hygiene methods work the same way

steps.activity:
Students rub fluorescent lotion (a model for germs) onto their hands. Each writes a prediction of which
method will remove the most: a 5-second water rinse, a 20-second soap wash, an alcohol hand sanitiser
rub, or wiping on paper towel, with reasons.
steps.formativeCheck: Written predictions with reasons

steps.activity: The class tallies predictions for each method.
steps.formativeCheck: Class tally displayed

steps.activity:
Groups each test one method, inspect hands under a UV torch, photograph the result and rate remaining
coverage on a simple scale.
steps.formativeCheck: Photographs and coverage ratings compared across groups

steps.activity:
Groups compare results with predictions. The class discusses mechanical removal versus killing microbes,
and the model's limitation: sanitiser can inactivate many microbes without removing the lotion. The
teacher links methods to modes of transmission and prevention.
steps.formativeCheck: Group explanations of the model's limitation

scaffoldSlots.prompt: What would a student say that shows they have concluded "sanitiser doesn't work" from the model? How would you respond?

steps.activity: Exit ticket: "I predicted… I observed… Now I think…", including one limitation of the model.
steps.formativeCheck: Exit tickets used to plan the transmission lesson

whyItWorks: The short water rinse reliably disappoints, contradicting a common belief
Groups generate their own visible, photographed evidence
The model's limitation turns a possible misconception into a Stage 5 discussion about models
The episode leads directly into teaching on transmission and prevention
workedSequences.watchFor:
Students concluding that sanitiser "doesn't work" because the lotion remains. Plan the explain step
around this limitation rather than letting it slip past.
workedSequences.safetyNotes:
This guide does not carry safety advice and is not a substitute for your school's risk assessment.
What this lesson introduces, so you know what to assess: a lotion applied to students' skin, which
raises sensitivities and allergies; UV torches; and alcohol-based hand sanitiser, which is flammable.
Take these to your head teacher or faculty safety contact and check them against your school's
practical procedures and current NSW guidance before you run anything.

One point specific to POE, and it cuts the other way from the open models. You supply the event, so
you know in advance exactly what will be in the room, which makes this the most straightforward kind
of practical to assess. The thing to watch is that the event is chosen to surprise the students — make
sure it does not also surprise you, particularly if you have adapted someone else's discrepant event
without running it first.
workedSequences.predictPrompt: Before reading on, where does the fluorescent-lotion model of germs break down, and why is that limitation useful in the explain step?

workedSequences.title: Will burning make it lighter?
workedSequences.bigQuestion: When something burns, where does the matter go, and what does energy have to do with it?
learningIntentions: Burning is a chemical change in which substances combine to form new ones
Mass is not lost in a chemical change; it can come from, or go into, the air
Energy is needed to start some chemical changes, and some changes release energy as they happen
targetConceptions: Burning destroys matter, so things always get lighter
A flame is a substance that is used up

steps.activity:
A loose ball of steel wool on a heatproof mat on a digital balance, under the visualiser. The teacher
records the mass, says it will be heated and weighed again, and every student writes what the balance
will read afterwards and why. Slips are collected before anything is lit.
steps.formativeCheck: Written predictions with reasons, collected unseen

scaffoldSlots.prompt: A student predicts the mass will go up "because burnt things are heavier". Is that the same understanding as the scientific one? What would you ask?

steps.activity:
The class tallies predictions (goes down, stays the same, goes up) without discussion. The teacher
adds one more question: what will it take to get it burning at all, and once it starts, will it
need more help to keep going?
steps.formativeCheck: Class tally on the board

steps.activity:
The teacher touches a 9 V battery to the steel wool, or holds a flame to it briefly, and lets the glow
spread. Students record the balance reading every thirty seconds, the colour and texture before and
after, and whether the glow keeps going on its own, in an observation column separate from their
interpretation.
steps.formativeCheck: Observation tables checked for separation of observation and inference

steps.activity:
Pairs compare prediction with observation and write what would have to be true for both. The teacher
consolidates: the iron combined with oxygen from the air to form a new substance, iron oxide, so the
mass gained is oxygen. The spark supplied the energy to start the change, and the glow spreading
on its own shows the change releases energy as it goes. She then asks why paper gets lighter when it
burns, and lets pairs answer with the same idea.
steps.formativeCheck: Revised explanations shared; the paper question answered by each pair

steps.activity: Exit ticket: "I predicted… I observed… Now I think… The energy came from…"
steps.formativeCheck: Exit tickets sorted to plan the next lesson

whyItWorks: The result is the opposite of what most students expect, and it is read off a balance everyone can see
The energy question is asked before lighting, so what starts and sustains the change is observed rather than told
The paper question after the explanation checks whether students have the idea or only the result
The exit ticket gives the teacher evidence to plan the next lesson
workedSequences.watchFor:
Steel wool that is packed too tightly will not burn through and gives a tiny change. Tease it out
loosely and run the demonstration beforehand on the same balance.
This episode covers the chemical half of Change. The geological half, energy driving weathering and the
rock cycle, needs its own lesson; the freeze–thaw example in the Explain phase is a ready starting point.
workedSequences.safetyNotes:
This guide does not carry safety advice and is not a substitute for your school's risk assessment.
What this sequence introduces, so you know what to assess: burning steel wool, which glows and can
drop hot fragments, beside a digital balance, with a battery or flame as the ignition source. Take this
to your head teacher or faculty safety contact and check it against your school's chemical and practical
procedures and current NSW guidance before you run anything.

One point specific to POE. You supply the event, so you know in advance exactly what will be in the
room. The thing to watch is that the event is chosen to surprise the students; make sure it does not
also surprise you by running it first with the same steel wool and balance.
workedSequences.predictPrompt: Before reading on, most of the class will predict the mass goes down. Why is it important that the slips are collected before the steel wool is lit, rather than discussed first?

workedSequences.title: Can water break a rock?
workedSequences.bigQuestion: How can something as soft as water break something as hard as rock?
learningIntentions: Water expands as it freezes, which is unusual; most substances contract as they cool
Freezing changes volume but not mass
Repeated freezing and thawing of water in cracks breaks rock apart, as energy is removed and added over and over
targetConceptions: Everything shrinks when it gets cold
Ice is heavier than the water it came from
Rock is too hard for water to break

steps.activity:
Two identical plastic bottles, each filled to the brim with water and capped. The teacher says one
went into the freezer yesterday afternoon and is still there. Every student writes what that bottle
will look like now, whether it will weigh more, less or the same as this one, and why.
steps.formativeCheck: Written predictions with reasons, collected unseen

scaffoldSlots.prompt: A student predicts the frozen bottle will be heavier "because ice is solid". What does that tell you, and which part of the Observe phase will test it?

steps.activity:
The class tallies predictions for shape (smaller, the same, bigger) and for mass, without discussion.
Most will predict it shrinks, because cooling makes things contract.
steps.formativeCheck: Class tallies on the board

steps.activity:
The frozen bottle comes out: bulging, the cap forced up, a dome of ice standing proud of the rim. Both
bottles go on the balance in turn. Then a plastic measuring cylinder, marked at its water level before it
was frozen, shows how far the ice has risen. Students record shape, mass and the two levels in an
observation column, separate from what they think it means.
steps.formativeCheck: Observation tables checked for measurements and for separation of observation and inference

steps.activity:
Pairs write what they predicted, what they saw and what would have to be true for both. The teacher
consolidates: water expands by about a tenth as it freezes, because ice forms an open structure; the
mass stays the same because nothing was added or taken away. She names the everything-shrinks idea
rather than leaving it unspoken. Then a photo of shattered rock on an alpine slope: pairs explain what
water in a crack would do on a frosty night, and what happens when it thaws and freezes again.
steps.formativeCheck: Each pair's explanation of the alpine photo, shared and compared

steps.activity: Exit ticket: "I predicted… I observed… Now I think… A rock with water in its cracks, after a hundred frosty nights, would…"
steps.formativeCheck: Exit tickets sorted to plan the next lesson

whyItWorks: The prediction runs against a rule students already trust, that cooling makes things shrink, so the result cannot be absorbed without thinking
Weighing both bottles separates volume from mass, which the heavier-ice idea confuses
The measuring cylinder turns a dramatic effect into a quantity, so "about a tenth" is something they saw
The alpine photo carries the result into geology, so the lesson answers the question it opened with
workedSequences.watchFor:
Freezing takes hours, so the frozen bottle and cylinder are prepared the day before, and a spare of
each is worth having in case one has leaked. Glass must not be used: it can shatter in the freezer.
This episode covers the geological half of Change. The chemical half is `ep-s4-steel-wool`; run the two
together and ask students where the energy went in each.
workedSequences.safetyNotes:
This guide does not carry safety advice and is not a substitute for your school's risk assessment.
What this sequence introduces, so you know what to assess: sealed plastic containers frozen until they
split, which can leave sharp edges; ice handled by students; and water on the floor near the balance.
Take these to your head teacher or faculty safety contact and check them against your school's practical
procedures and current NSW guidance before you run anything.

One point specific to POE. You supply the event, so you know in advance exactly what will be in the
room. Make sure the event does not also surprise you: freeze a test bottle first, in the same freezer.
workedSequences.predictPrompt: Before reading on, students predict the frozen bottle and weigh it in the same lesson. Why ask about mass as well as shape, when the lesson is about breaking rock?

misapplications.name: No real surprise
misapplications.looksLike: An event most students predict correctly.
misapplications.whyItUndermines: Without a mismatch there is no pressure to change ideas.
misapplications.fix: Choose events from documented alternative conceptions, and trial them with a colleague.

misapplications.name: Predictions without reasons
misapplications.looksLike: Students record only what they think will happen.
misapplications.whyItUndermines: The underlying idea never surfaces, so there is nothing to revise.
misapplications.fix: Require a because statement for every prediction.

misapplications.name: Cued predictions
misapplications.looksLike: Wording or tone signals the expected answer.
misapplications.whyItUndermines: Students predict what they think the teacher wants, hiding their real ideas.
misapplications.fix: Present the set-up neutrally and collect predictions before any hint.

misapplications.name: An observation students can dismiss
misapplications.looksLike: A small, unclear or unrepeatable effect.
misapplications.whyItUndermines: Students explain away the result rather than their prediction.
misapplications.fix: Make the result visible and checkable, and repeat it on request.

misapplications.name: POE as a quiz
misapplications.looksLike: The teacher asks who got it right and moves on.
misapplications.whyItUndermines: Wrong predictors feel judged and no one revises their thinking.
misapplications.fix: Treat every prediction as useful evidence of thinking, and spend most time on explanation.

misapplications.name: A one-off demonstration
misapplications.looksLike: A POE with no link to the lessons that follow.
misapplications.whyItUndermines: Conflict without follow-up rarely produces lasting change.
misapplications.fix: Keep predictions and revisit them in the next lessons.

items.text: The event targets a documented alternative conception
The event has been trialled and works reliably
The event has a risk assessment
Every student writes a prediction before observing
The set-up is presented without cues
Every student can see or check the result
Observations are recorded separately from inferences
Students compare prediction and observation explicitly
Students revise their explanations before the teacher consolidates
A follow-up lesson builds on the conflict
Sentence frames are available for predictions and explanations
The classroom treats wrong predictions as valuable, not embarrassing

wsMapping.note: A POE gives students no planning role. Extend it with a follow-up in which students design their own test of the idea.
Only when students run the event themselves rather than watching a demonstration.
Not a problem-solving strategy. Pair it with a design or problem-based task if WS-07 is a target.

syllabusAlignment.depthStudies: A surprising POE result is a strong source of student questions for a depth study.
syllabusAlignment.dataScience: A class tally of predictions is a small data set; comparing predicted and observed distributions is an accessible Data science link.

inclusion.eald: Offer sentence frames ("I predict… because…", "I observed…", "Now I think…") and allow drawings as predictions.
inclusion.disability: Ensure the observation is accessible, for example through a visualiser, tactile or audio cues, or hands-on sets.
inclusion.highPotential: Ask students to predict a quantitative result, or to design a second event that tests the same idea.
inclusion.aboriginalPerspectives: Where appropriate, draw events from local contexts and knowledges, such as fermentation or seasonal indicators, developed with community.

nesting.how: Use a POE as the Engage to surface and challenge the target conception.
Use a POE to stage the challenge between students' views and the scientific view.
Use a POE to prompt students' first explanatory models.
Use the guidance dial to decide whether students run the event themselves or observe a demonstration.
Use a POE before the guiding question is posed, to surface prior ideas.
Use a POE as the 7E hook, once Elicit has shown which conception to target.

reflectionPrompts.prompt: Recall a time a result surprised you in science. Did it change your mind straight away? What else had to happen?
coachFollowUps: What made you trust or doubt the result?
How long did the change take?

reflectionPrompts.prompt: Chinn and Brewer (1993) show that students often reject or reinterpret anomalous data. What does that imply for how much weight a single POE can carry?
